sections.html:
Cedar Rapids is both the biggest city and the seat of Linn County, which lies in eastern Iowa. The county's 230,299 people (2020 count) make it the second most populous in the state.

After Cedar Rapids at 137,710, the biggest cities are Marion at 41,535, Hiawatha at 7,183, Mount Vernon at 4,527 and Robins at 3,353.

Selling here starts with one practical question: which assessor covers your house? The answer changes at the Cedar Rapids city line, and the next section sorts it out.

Inside Cedar Rapids, the City Assessor values your house. Outside the city limits, the Linn County Assessor takes over. Neither one collects tax or sets the rate. The City Assessor's office says as much itself, and the county assessor's work is likewise about value, with taxing bodies setting budgets and levies. The state Department of Revenue, not either local office, values utilities and railroads.

  • Linn County Assessor (linn.iowaassessors.com): values real property and revalues in odd-numbered years, so every second year. Its assessment date is January 1.
  • Cedar Rapids City Assessor (500 15th Avenue SW, 319-286-5888): covers property inside the city and revalues annually.
  • Linn County Treasurer (935 Second St. SW, 319-892-5500): takes payments, conducts the tax sale and processes redemptions.
  • Board of Review: hears protests. It has five members chosen by the Conference Board, and you reach it through the assessor's office.

Value is fixed on January 1, tax comes due in two installments, and protest season is April.

DateWhat happens
January 1Assessment date
By April 1Assessors finish and notify owners
April 2 to 25Informal assessor hearings can be requested
April 2 to 30Protests filed with the Board of Review
May 1 to 31Board of Review considers protests
September 30 and March 31First and second installments payable
October 1Final equalization orders issued
October 9 to 31Equalization protests to the board
Third Monday in JuneCounty tax sale of unpaid parcels

A spring payment needs a March 31 postmark and a fall payment needs September 30. Interest on a delinquent installment is 1.5 percent monthly.

Your written protest must reach the Board of Review from April 2 through April 30 in the assessment year, and the board cannot extend that window. Declared disaster areas are the lone exception, with filing from May 1 to June 5 (Iowa Code 441.37).

Pick from five statutory grounds:

  • Similar property in your taxing district is assessed lower.
  • Your value exceeds what the law allows.
  • The property is not assessable, is exempt, or is classified wrongly.
  • The assessor made an error.
  • Fraud or misconduct occurred, and you must describe it specifically.

An oral hearing happens only if you request it, in writing, at the time you file. If several parcels share the same grounds, a single form can cover them. When the board rules, it sends written notice of what it did and why.

You can pay online, by mail, in a drop box, by phone, or at the counter of the Treasurer at 935 Second St. SW, Cedar Rapids. Checks are written to the Linn County Treasurer. Send the stub torn from your statement along with the check so it posts to the correct parcel.

  • Paying cash or a check at the counter adds no fee.
  • Online, checks cost $0.30, debit cards cost $3.25 plus $0.30 a transaction, and credit cards cost 2.20 percent plus $0.30 a transaction.
  • Cash cannot be paid online.
  • Lobby hours are Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., except the second Wednesday of each month, when the lobby opens at 10 a.m.

Watch the mail. USPS now postmarks an envelope on the day it is processed, not the day you drop it off, so a late-processed letter can count as late. A manual postmark from a staffed retail counter is free and protects you.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax when you sell
sections.html:
An unpaid installment does not vanish when the house changes hands, so it gets settled at closing. The current installment is split the way your purchase contract says. Delinquent amounts come out of what you receive, leaving the buyer with title free of them.

In practice the order of events is simple. Call the Treasurer for a balance before listing and pass that figure to the title company. The payoff then appears on your settlement statement. When you meet the closing agent, take your latest tax statement and any delinquency notice so nobody has to guess. Ask also whether any tax suspension or clearance letter applies to your parcel, since those can affect the closing date.

The Treasurer's office also issues plat and mobile home clearances and processes tax suspensions, which can come up around a sale. The state transfer tax is 80 cents per $500 of value beyond the first $500, and it falls on the seller as grantor (Iowa Code 428A.1 and 428A.3).

Taxes that stay unpaid long enough are offered at the June tax sale. The Treasurer conducts it, processes redemptions and issues the tax sale deeds. To get a sold parcel back you pay the sold amount plus 2 percent interest per month. Our statewide Iowa tax deed and tax lien sales guide walks through the redemption steps.

Cash Home Buyers buys Linn County houses as-is, including ones with tax issues, and we confirm numbers with you before any offer. A cash sale avoids repairs and showings, and back taxes are paid from the price at closing. If you are sitting on several years of unpaid installments, tell us up front. The sooner the real balance is known, the sooner you can decide between redeeming, listing, or selling for cash, and the June sale date is the clock that matters most.

sections.h2: Older Cedar Rapids houses and past damage
sections.html:
On June 13, 2008 the Cedar River peaked at a record 31.12 feet, and on August 10, 2020 a derecho hit the county. Cedar Rapids housing still shows both. An older house may carry history from repairs made after either one.

If yours does, gather permits, contractor invoices and insurance paperwork before you talk to any buyer. Paperwork like this answers a traditional buyer's inspector quickly. An as-is cash buyer will take the house in its present condition and skip the repair haggling.

faqs.q: Who assesses property in Cedar Rapids?
faqs.a: The Cedar Rapids City Assessor, from the City Services Center at 500 15th Avenue SW. The Linn County Assessor covers real property in the rest of the county.

faqs.q: When are Linn County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due September 1 and payable through September 30. The second half is due March 1 and payable through March 31. Payments must be postmarked by those dates.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to protest a Linn County assessment?
faqs.a: April 30 of the assessment year, with filing opening April 2. Declared disaster areas get May 1 through June 5.

faqs.q: What late interest applies in Linn County?
faqs.a: Delinquent installments accrue 1.5 percent interest per month. A payment that arrives without a valid postmark can also draw a 1.5 percent late fee.

faqs.q: Where do I call the Linn County Treasurer?
faqs.a: Call 319-892-5500, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Hold times can be long, so a visit or an appointment at the Public Service Center is sometimes faster.
